title: Deep Feed-Forward Networks & Backprop
oneLiner: Stacking simple decision-makers so a network can learn curved, complicated patterns, and teaching it by passing blame backwards.

what.html:
A deep feed-forward network is a stack of layers made of tiny calculators called neurons. Each neuron does three things:

  1. Weigh its inputs (some matter more than others),
  2. add them up,
  3. bend the result with an activation function.

Information flows one way only, from input to output, like an assembly line. There are no loops. That's what "feed-forward" means. "Deep" means there is at least one hidden layer between input and output.

Everyday versionThink of a company. Junior staff each look at a small piece of raw data. Team leads combine their reports into patterns. A director combines those into a final decision. No one person sees everything, but together they make sophisticated calls.

why.html:
A single neuron can only draw one straight line to separate things. Many real problems can't be split by one straight line.

The staircase lightA staircase light has a switch at the bottom and one at the top. The light is on when exactly one switch is up. Plot the four switch combinations and try to separate "on" from "off" with a single ruler: you can't. This is the XOR problem from the slides, and it is why we need hidden layers.

Images, speech, language and medical diagnosis are all full of curvy, tangled patterns like this. Hidden layers let the network build its own new features, so tangled data becomes separable.

how.title: One neuron = one straight line
how.html:
A single neuron computes "weight × input + weight × input + bias" and says yes if the total is positive. On a 2-D map that is exactly one straight line.

Try the One neuron tab: whatever you do, you can get at most 3 of the 4 XOR points right. Then switch to Two hidden neurons.

how.title: Hidden neurons re-draw the map
how.html:
With two hidden neurons, each draws its own line. The output neuron no longer looks at the original map. It looks at the hidden neurons' answers, which is a new map where the XOR points line up so that one straight line works.

That's the core trick of deep learning: each layer re-describes the data in a way that makes the next layer's job easier.

how.title: Why the bend matters
how.html:
If neurons only weighed and added, stacking ten layers would still be one big weighted sum: one straight line again. The activation function adds a bend after each layer, and bends stacked on bends can make any shape.

Folding paperFolding a sheet once makes one crease. Fold, then fold again, and you can make complex shapes. Each layer with an activation adds a fold.
  • ReLU: "if negative, output 0; otherwise pass it through". Cheap, and the modern default for hidden layers.
  • Sigmoid: squashes anything into 0–1, which is handy for a yes/no probability at the output.
  • Tanh: squashes into −1 to 1.

how.title: Four ingredients of every network
how.html:
1. DataExamples with answers.
2. ModelThe stack of layers.
3. Scoring ruleA loss that says how wrong a prediction is.
4. Learning methodBackprop + gradient descent to improve the weights.

It's the same recipe as linear regression, with more layers and bends.

how.title: Forward pass: the assembly line
how.html:
To make a prediction, the input goes through layer 1, its output goes to layer 2, and so on until the last layer gives the answer. Each step is "weigh, add, bend". Prediction after training is just this forward pass.

How big is the network? Every connection has a weight and every neuron a bias. The slides' digit classifier (784 pixels → 256 → 128 → 10 digits) has 235,146 adjustable numbers.

how.title: Scoring the mistake
how.html:
The scoring rule depends on the question being asked:

  • Predicting a number? Squared error, as in regression.
  • Yes or no? Cross-entropy. It barely punishes "90% sure and right" but heavily punishes "99% sure and wrong". Confident mistakes are expensive.
  • Which of 10 classes? Softmax turns scores into probabilities that add to 1, and categorical cross-entropy scores them.

how.title: Backpropagation: passing blame backwards
how.html:
After a wrong prediction, every weight should change a little, but by how much and in which direction? Backprop answers this by passing blame backwards from the output.

The post-mortem meetingThe director knows how wrong the final decision was. They tell each team lead how much their report contributed. Each team lead then works out how much each junior's input contributed. Blame flows backwards along the same paths the information came forward.

The maths is the chain rule: blame gets multiplied along each path. The clever part is that one backward sweep computes the blame for every weight at once, which is why training millions of weights is possible.

Backprop only computes the directions. Gradient descent then takes the step.

how.title: Learning in small batches
how.html: Rather than looking at all the data before each step, the network looks at a mini-batch (typically 32–256 examples), computes the average blame, takes a step, and moves on. One pass through all the data is an epoch.

how.title: Deep vs wide
how.html:
Wide = more neurons in a layer. Deep = more layers.

Depth builds a hierarchy. In an image network the early layers spot edges, the middle layers combine edges into shapes, and later layers recognise objects. A famous theorem says one huge hidden layer can in principle learn any pattern, but it may need an enormous number of neurons. Depth gets there with far fewer.

how.title: When very deep networks struggle
how.html:
• Vanishing gradients: like the telephone game, the blame message fades as it passes back through many layers, so early layers stop learning. ReLU and careful initialisation help.
  • Exploding gradients: the opposite. The message gets louder each layer until numbers blow up. Clipping helps.
  • Degradation: very deep plain networks can train worse than shallower ones. Skip connections (ResNets) fix this.

how.title: A practical recipe
how.html:
• Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: match the task (none for numbers, sigmoid for yes/no, softmax for classes).
  • Start small (2–3 hidden layers), grow only if needed.
  • Initialise weights randomly, never all zeros. Identical twins given identical lessons stay identical: zero-initialised neurons would all learn the same thing.
  • Standardise inputs. Watch training and validation loss; stop when validation loss starts rising.
  • Sanity check: a good network should be able to memorise a tiny batch.

demo.html:
Train a real neural network in your browser on a 2-D problem. The background colour is what the network currently predicts at every point. Things to try:

  • Pick Rings and set hidden neurons to 1. It can only draw a straight-ish boundary. Raise it to 6 and watch it wrap around the centre.
  • Switch the activation to Linear (no bend). Even with many neurons the boundary stays a straight line, the slides' point about non-linearity.
  • Push the learning rate very high and watch the loss jump around.

example.html:
Reading handwritten digits. The slides' example network takes a 28 × 28 image (784 pixel values), passes it through hidden layers of 256 and 128 neurons, and outputs 10 probabilities, one per digit. Early layers learn strokes and curves; later layers combine them into "this looks like a 7".

Supplementary The same structure classifies network alarms in telecom operations: feed in counters and KPIs, and the output layer gives a probability for each fault type.

misunderstandings: More layers always means a better model.
Deeper nets are harder to train and overfit small datasets. Start small.
Initialising all weights to zero is a neutral, safe start.
Every neuron in a layer then gets identical updates forever. Use random initialisation (Xavier or He).
Backprop computes the gradients. An optimiser such as SGD uses them to update the weights.
Sigmoid is a good choice for every layer.
In hidden layers it saturates and causes vanishing gradients. Use ReLU there and keep sigmoid for a binary output.
takeaways: A neuron weighs, adds and bends. One neuron can only draw a straight line.
Hidden layers re-describe the data so tangled problems like XOR become separable.
Without non-linear activations, any stack of layers collapses to a single linear model.
Training = forward pass → loss → backprop (blame flows backwards via the chain rule) → gradient-descent update, in mini-batches.
Depth builds hierarchies efficiently, but very deep nets need ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation and skip connections.
thirty: A deep feed-forward network is layers of neurons that each weigh their inputs, add them, and bend the result. One neuron can only draw a straight line, but hidden layers re-map the data so curved patterns like XOR become simple. To learn, the network makes a prediction, scores the mistake with a loss, then backpropagation passes blame backwards through the layers using the chain rule, and gradient descent nudges every weight. ReLU, random initialisation and mini-batches make this work in practice.

check.q: Why can't a single neuron solve XOR?
opts: It can only draw one straight boundary
It needs a bigger learning rate
check.why: XOR's classes sit on opposite corners, so no single line separates them.

check.q: What happens if you remove every activation function from a 10-layer network?
opts: It becomes ten times more powerful
It behaves like a single linear model
check.why: A chain of linear maps is still one linear map.
It computes gradients; the optimiser applies the update.

check.q: Which output fits a 'which of 10 digits?' question?
check.why: Softmax gives 10 probabilities that sum to 1.

check.q: Why not start with all weights at zero?
opts: Zero is not a valid number for weights
All neurons in a layer would learn the same thing
check.why: Symmetric starts give identical gradients, so neurons never differentiate.
